title: Smartwatch irregular-rhythm notifications send a 25-year-old man to the emergency department, where atrial fibrillation is confirmed and cardioverted
summary: A 25-year-old's smartwatch notified him several times of an irregular rhythm consistent with AF; ECG showed AF with rapid ventricular response, treated by TEE-guided cardioversion (Cureus, 2023).
account: Bedi, Al Masri, Al Hennawi, Qadir and Ottman, internal medicine physicians at Abington Jefferson Hospital, Abington, USA (with a co-author at Alfaisal University, Riyadh), reported in Cureus on 9 March 2023 (the event date is not given, so the publication date is used) a 25-year-old man with anxiety and depression who presented to an emergency department with 24 hours of chest pressure and palpitations after his smartwatch had notified him several times of an irregular heart rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation, which the authors link to weekend binge drinking. He was tachycardic above 120 bpm; the ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response at 123 bpm. Intravenous diltiazem and oral metoprolol did not restore rhythm; enoxaparin was started; BNP was 796 with a clear chest X-ray. He was admitted, and on the cardiologist's recommendation underwent transoesophageal-echo-guided electrical cardioversion the next day, restoring sinus rhythm. Despite a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0 he was given apixaban for four weeks, advised on alcohol cessation and gradual return to exercise, and scheduled for monthly cardiology follow-up. The report does not name the watch's brand or model; it describes smartwatches generically as using photoplethysmography with deep neural network algorithms.
purpose: Smartwatch irregular-rhythm notifications are built to prompt the wearer to seek medical review; this benefit was that purpose.
system: Smartwatch irregular-rhythm notification (brand and model not stated)
developer: Not stated (the report does not name the device's maker)
location: Abington, United States (authors' hospital; the report does not name the emergency department)
taxonomy_note: None of the six types names a health outcome; chosen, as for the other wearable records, because the device made rhythm monitoring available outside clinical settings, which is what brought the patient to care. Brand unstated in the full text (checked: Apple is mentioned only in the discussion of published studies), so the case cannot be assigned to a brand record, as the earlier verifier noted.

ratings.reason: A 25-year-old received an ECG-confirmed AF diagnosis, cardioversion to sinus rhythm and four weeks of anticoagulation; a material benefit to one person, not described as life-saving.

ai_role.statement: The watch's own notification, repeated several times, is what the report says prompted the visit; clinicians confirmed AF on a 12-lead ECG and chose cardioversion. The brand is unknown, so the algorithm behind the notification cannot be identified; the authors describe smartwatch rhythm detection generically as deep-neural-network analysis of pulse waves.

produced_by: A wearer with symptomatic AF whose smartwatch issued repeated irregular-rhythm notifications
The wearer acting on the notifications by attending an emergency department
Clinicians confirming the rhythm on a 12-lead ECG and treating it
must_hold: The watch's notification corresponds to a true arrhythmia (the authors cite a positive predictive value of 84% for irregular-pulse notifications in the Apple Heart Study)
The wearer treats the notification as a reason to seek care

echoes.setting: Apple Heart Study, cited in the report's discussion: 34% of participants alerted to an irregular rhythm were later diagnosed with AF, positive predictive value 84%
